text: Streptococcosis in Nile tilapia may present with lethargy, erratic swimming, dark skin, bulging or opaque eyes, haemorrhage and abdominal distension.
Spiralling or spinning, loss of buoyancy, pop-eye and haemorrhage are frequent observations in streptococcal infections of fish because these bacteria may involve the brain and nervous system.
Stressors associated with streptococcal outbreaks include high water temperature, high stocking density, handling and poor water quality such as high ammonia or nitrite.

A tentative streptococcal diagnosis can combine history, signs, necropsy and Gram-positive cocci in fresh internal tissue; confirmation requires culture and identification, particularly from brain or kidney.
Surface gasping is not specific for streptococcosis. Dissolved oxygen and other water parameters must be checked because environmental distress can resemble infection.

Motile Aeromonas Septicemia in Nile tilapia may cause loss of equilibrium, lethargic swimming, surface gasping, inflamed or haemorrhaged fins and skin, bulging eyes, opaque corneas and abdominal swelling.
Aeromonas hydrophila is common in freshwater aquaculture environments and is generally opportunistic, so its presence alone does not establish that it caused disease in healthy fish.
A fish diagnostic work-up commonly includes water chemistry, external biopsies, necropsy and bacterial culture from kidney or other affected internal organs.
Haemorrhage, abdominal swelling and lethargy overlap with other systemic infections. A laboratory isolate and the complete case context are needed before attributing disease to Aeromonas.
Before disease treatment, record the case history and test water quality because environmental and infectious causes can coexist and prior treatment can make diagnosis more difficult.
Columnaris in Nile tilapia may present with frayed fins, irregular whitish-to-grey patches on the skin or fins, and pale necrotic lesions on the gills.
When gills are visibly damaged, respiratory distress can support a gill disease such as columnaris, but gasping alone is not disease-specific and requires water-quality assessment.
Fresh skin, fin and gill biopsies may reveal some columnaris-causing bacteria, while bacterial culture and other laboratory methods may be required for confirmation.
Neurological swimming, pop-eye and haemorrhage without characteristic skin or gill patches are less typical of columnaris and should broaden the differential.
Photograph external lesions, minimise handling, measure water quality and obtain diagnostic samples before assuming that visible skin changes identify a single pathogen.

TiLV clinical signs are variable and non-specific; reported findings include lethargy, loss of appetite, exophthalmia, body-colour change, skin erosion with haemorrhage, scale protrusion and abdominal distension.
TiLV disease has been associated with transfer between ponds and may be associated with transfer stress; infected farmed and wild fish populations are established reservoirs.
TiLV confirmation may use RT-PCR or RT-qPCR, histopathology and virus isolation in a qualified laboratory; gross signs alone do not confirm infection.
Potential TiLV diagnostic tissues include liver, brain, spleen, kidney, heart, gills and muscle. Sample condition and preservation affect which tests remain useful.
Unusual tilapia mortality with compatible signs should prompt biosecurity, recording of stock movements and consultation with aquatic animal-health authorities or a diagnostic laboratory.

text: FAO training material lists dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L as optimal for Nile tilapia and states that poor water quality may suppress immunity and increase disease and mortality risk.
FAO training material lists unionised ammonia (NH3) below 0.1 mg/L as optimal for Nile tilapia. Total ammonia and unionised ammonia must not be treated as interchangeable measurements.

Abnormal behaviour worth recording includes gasping, crowding near water inlets or outlets, lethargy, erratic or circular swimming and loss of appetite; these findings are observations rather than a diagnosis.
Environmental triage should measure dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite, pH and temperature and review recent aeration, filtration, feeding and water-management events.

A rapid event affecting most fish within about a day often suggests an environmental cause, while persistent or progressive disease-specific lesions warrant investigation for infection or mixed causes.
Nile tilapia experimentally challenged with Aeromonas hydrophila showed erratic movement, scale loss, exophthalmia, tail erosion, skin redness and haemorrhage near the operculum.
In the study, Aeromonas hydrophila isolates were assessed by culture and biochemical characteristics, with selected isolates identified using a species-specific 16S rRNA PCR assay.
Nile tilapia exposed to Flavobacterium columnare showed gross external findings including scale loss, scale discoloration, skin lesions and haemorrhage.
Nile tilapia experimentally injected with TiLV showed gross external findings including abdominal swelling and exophthalmia.
